extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of history and philosophy of science; practitioners interested in the design and evaluation of decisive experiments (inductive method)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on constructing and evaluating 'instantiae crucis' (crucial instances) and related inductive tests: how to frame decisive experiments that discriminate between rival hypotheses, account for confounders, and respect context limits. Draws on Baconian methodology with historical examples (tides, rotation, gas tests, clocks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Crucial Instance (Instantiae Crucis)
rubrics_metrics.description: An observation or experiment which is 'decisive' between two or more rival hypotheses — a 'crux' that, by agreeing with one hypothesis and not with others, enables us to summarily reject the rest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: chemical tests to determine a substance's nature; Torricelli/Pascal mountain barometer experiment deciding the role of air weight. Most crucial instances are specially invented for the purpose rather than merely found. Use such instances to indicate logical bifurcations ('erectae in biviis indicant et signant viarum separationes').

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete (Two‑Way) vs Unilateral (One‑Way) Tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish tests that are decisive both ways (complete) from those that only give evidence in one direction (unilateral); many errors arise from mistaking unilateral tests for complete ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: flame burning in a gas is a rough unilateral indication of oxygen (burn => oxygen likely), but failure to burn does not prove absence of oxygen. A 'perfect test' (e.g., weighing a gas) would be decisive both ways. Warn against drawing symmetric conclusions from asymmetric tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Difference (Variation of One Circumstance)
rubrics_metrics.description: All other circumstances being the same, the appearance or disappearance of some one circumstance (or combination) enables determination of causation for the observed effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments that hold background conditions constant while changing only the candidate causal factor; this is the basis of method-of-difference experiments and is explicitly recommended as a way to 'determine the question at issue.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructed (Invented) Instances over Passive Observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Crucial instances are commonly 'made, not found' — they are often produced by contriving specific conditions or experiments to expose the causal relation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be proactive in designing experiments tailored to discriminate hypotheses (e.g., contrive circumstances similar to Torricelli/Pascal rather than waiting for a fortuitous observation). The text emphasizes deliberate invention and application ('de industria atque ex composito quaesitae et applicatae').

rubrics_metrics.name: Triaging Alternative Mechanistic Hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple mechanistic explanations are possible (e.g., tides caused by extra water, expansion/rarification, or magnetic attraction), set up decisive observations or experiments that distinguish among them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerate mutually exclusive candidate mechanisms and derive distinct observational consequences for each; then design or seek instances that would obtain under one mechanism but not the others (the text reduces the inquiry for tides to three possible modes and proposes tests to discriminate them).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consilience Across Media, Scales, and Systems
rubrics_metrics.description: A convincing crucial instance often involves the same motion/effect being found across different media and scales (ocean, air, comets, planets) with systematic variation (e.g., gradation with distance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example from rotation: if a motion from E→W is found weakly in the ocean, stronger in the air, stronger in comets, and gradated in planets (slower near earth, faster far away), this consilience supports the hypothesis that diurnal motion is real in the heavens and not motion of the earth. Use cross-system, scale-sensitive evidence to strengthen inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for Contextual and Derivative Limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize contexts where phenomena are derivative (e.g., tides in narrow straits, 'in fretis') and where experiments therefore cannot be conclusive for global causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid applying a crucial-instance test in settings where the measured phenomenon is a local derivative or confounded manifestation; note when an experiment is non-conclusive because the site produces secondary effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Geographically Comparative Observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare synchronous observations from different geographic locales (e.g., coasts on opposite sides of an isthmus) to test global hypotheses about causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: query inhabitants of Panama and Lima or compare tides at opposite coasts to decide whether tides are due to progressive motion or other causes. Geographic comparison can reveal whether effects are globally consistent with a proposed mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: State and Test Background Assumptions Explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and make explicit auxiliary assumptions (e.g., terrestrial immobility) required for an instance to be decisive, and test or acknowledge them when interpreting results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The conclusiveness of some instances depends on assumptions — e.g., some tidal inferences assume the earth is immobile; if such assumptions are false (earth rotates), the interpretation changes. Either justify assumptions or design tests independent of them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of Confounders and Equifinality (Different Causes Yielding Same Phenomenon)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that different hypotheses may produce the same observable outcomes unless experiments are designed to discriminate them; experimental conditions must avoid being equally compatible with rival accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: conditions proposed to reject earth's motion might equally suit either hypothesis because of planetary proper motions; hence, ensure that an instance would produce divergent outcomes under competing theories, not identical ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete Mechanical Analogues as Tests (Instrumental Experiments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use mechanical or instrumental comparisons (e.g., clocks moved by different principles placed at different heights) as crucial instances to test causal theories about forces like gravity or attraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: compare a clock driven by weights with one driven by compression of an iron plate, place one at a high temple summit and the other low, and see whether rates differ as predicted by attraction-vs-intrinsic-scheme accounts of weight. Mechanical analogues can operationalize theoretical contrasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational Morphology as Diagnostic Evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Use morphological features of phenomena (e.g., curvature/roundness of sea surface during ebb vs flood) as diagnostic signs to infer underlying mechanisms (e.g., magnetic uplift).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if during reflux the sea surface is more arched/rounded in the middle and lower at the sides (littora), and in flux the surface is flatter, this pattern might be taken as decisive for a particular mechanism (sublation by magnetic force). Such morphological diagnostics can serve as crucial instances when tied to theoretical predictions.
